markingPoints.description: Notes that similar foods were also known in India and Japan
States that the truth about their origins may never be known
Explains that such guesswork suggests only the possibilities of long-distance cultural contact

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Because similar foods were also known in India and Japan, several explanations fit the evidence equally well. questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student is studying the silk routes as a clear case of trade and cultural exchange going hand in hand; name the three different groups or movements that travelled or spread along these routes, and say what their use of the routes suggests.

markingPoints.description: Names Christian missionaries as having travelled the route to Asia
Names early Muslim preachers as having travelled it a few centuries later
Places the emergence of Buddhism in eastern India
Notes that Buddhism spread in several directions through intersecting points on the silk routes
Concludes that trade and cultural exchange went hand in hand, so the routes carried religion and ideas as well as goods

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Christian missionaries almost certainly travelled the route to Asia, and early Muslim preachers travelled it a few centuries later. Much before all of them, Buddhism emerged from eastern India and spread in several directions through intersecting points on the silk routes. Their use of the routes shows that trade and cultural exchange went hand in hand: these were not merely trading roads, but routes along which religion travelled and spread too.

evidence: Trade and cultural exchange always went hand in hand. Early
Christian missionaries almost certainly travelled this route to Asia, as

did early Muslim preachers a few centuries later. Much before all
this, Buddhism emerged from eastern India and spread in several
directions through intersecting points on the silk routes.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student is asked to explain, step by step, why the pre-modern world shrank greatly in the sixteenth century; give (a) what European sailors achieved, (b) what the trade in the Indian Ocean had already been like for centuries before, and (c) what the entry of Europeans did to those flows.

markingPoints.description: States that European sailors found a sea route to Asia
States that they also successfully crossed the western ocean to America
Describes the Indian Ocean's centuries of bustling trade, with goods, people, knowledge and customs criss-crossing its waters
Places the Indian subcontinent at the centre of these flows and as a crucial point in their networks
States that the entry of the Europeans helped expand or redirect some of these flows towards Europe

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) European sailors found a sea route to Asia and also successfully crossed the western ocean to America.
(b) For centuries before, the Indian Ocean had known a bustling trade, with goods, people, knowledge and customs criss-crossing its waters. The Indian subcontinent was central to these flows and a crucial point in their networks.
(c) The entry of the Europeans helped expand or redirect some of these flows towards Europe, so that the pre-modern world shrank greatly.

evidence:
The pre-modern world shrank greatly in the sixteenth century after
European sailors found a sea route to Asia and also successfully
crossed the western ocean to America. For centuries before, the

Indian Ocean had known a bustling trade, with goods, people,
knowledge, customs, etc. criss-crossing its waters. The Indian
subcontinent was central to these flows and a crucial point in their

networks. The entry of the Europeans helped expand or redirect
some of these flows towards Europe.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student is asked why European conquest of America cannot be put down to superior firepower alone; show in steps (a) what the most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors actually was, (b) how it reached the people they conquered, and (c) why those people were unable to resist it.

markingPoints.description: States that the most powerful weapon was not a conventional military weapon at all
Identifies germs such as those of smallpox as the weapon
Notes that the germs were carried on the conquerors' persons
Explains that because of their long isolation, America's original inhabitants had no immunity against these diseases
Concludes that conquest therefore owed as much to disease as to superior firepower

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) The most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors was not a conventional military weapon at all.
(b) It was germs such as those of smallpox, which they carried on their person.
(c) Because of their long isolation, America's original inhabitants had no immunity against these diseases. This is why European conquest was not just a result of superior firepower, but of disease spreading ahead of the conquerors.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.topic: Rebuilding a World Economy: The Post-war Era
questions.stem: A student is tracing why the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates could no longer be maintained; show in steps (a) how the system originally worked, (b) what went wrong with the US dollar, and (c) what system replaced it.

markingPoints.description: States that national currencies, for example the Indian rupee, were pegged to the dollar at a fixed exchange rate
States that the dollar itself was anchored to gold at a fixed price of $35 per ounce of gold
Notes that from the 1960s the rising costs of the US's overseas involvements weakened its finances and competitive strength
States that the US dollar no longer commanded confidence as the world's principal currency and could not maintain its value in relation to gold
States that this led to the collapse of the system of fixed exchange rates and the introduction of a system of floating exchange rates

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) National currencies, for example the Indian rupee, were pegged to the dollar at a fixed exchange rate, and the dollar was anchored to gold at a fixed price of $35 per ounce.
(b) From the 1960s the rising costs of the US's overseas involvements weakened its finances and competitive strength; the US dollar no longer commanded confidence and could not maintain its value in relation to gold.
(c) This led to the collapse of the system of fixed exchange rates and the introduction of a system of floating exchange rates.

questions.stem:
Historians have identified several silk routes, over land and by sea, knitting together vast regions of Asia and linking Asia with Europe and northern Africa. They are known to have existed since before the Christian Era and thrived almost till the fifteenth century. Chinese pottery also travelled the same route, as did textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia. In return, precious metals – gold and silver – flowed from Europe to Asia. Christian missionaries almost certainly travelled this route to Asia, and early Muslim preachers a few centuries later.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one line. (i) Name the two ways in which the routes described here were used. (ii) Which regions sent textiles and spices along them, and what came back the other way? (iii) A trader argues that these were only roads for buying and selling. Explain why the journeys of the missionaries and preachers show otherwise.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Over land and by sea. (ii) India and Southeast Asia sent textiles and spices; precious metals – gold and silver – flowed in return from Europe to Asia. (iii) Because missionaries and preachers travelled the same routes to spread religion, trade and cultural exchange went hand in hand, so these were not merely trading roads.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
Many of our common foods such as potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes were not known to our ancestors until about five centuries ago. These foods were only introduced in Europe and Asia after Christopher Columbus accidentally discovered the vast continent that would later become known as the Americas. Europe’s poor began to eat better and live longer with the introduction of the humble potato. Ireland’s poorest peasants became so dependent on potatoes that when disease destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands died of starvation.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one line. (i) Name the people from whom many of these foods came. (ii) State the two changes the humble potato brought to Europe. (iii) A student says the new foods were a simple benefit; use the Irish experience in the case to explain why that is not the whole story.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) America’s original inhabitants, the American Indians. (ii) Europe’s poor began to eat better, and they lived longer. (iii) Ireland’s poorest peasants became so dependent on potatoes that when disease destroyed the crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands died of starvation, so one new crop could carry great risk as well as great gain.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
The Portuguese and Spanish conquest and colonisation of America was decisively under way by the mid-sixteenth century. European conquest was not just a result of superior firepower. The most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors was not a conventional military weapon at all: it was germs such as those of smallpox that they carried on their person. Because of their long isolation, America’s original inhabitants had no immunity against these diseases. Before its ‘discovery’, America had been cut off from regular contact with the rest of the world for millions of years.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one or two lines. (i) Name the weapon the Spanish conquerors really relied on, and say how it reached the people they met. (ii) Why were those people unable to resist it? (iii) A historian argues that isolation, rather than any weakness, explains why conquest succeeded so quickly; explain what in the case supports that argument.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Germs such as those of smallpox, which they carried on their own persons. (ii) Because of their long isolation, America’s original inhabitants had no immunity against these diseases. (iii) So conquest was not merely a result of superior firepower: the germs reached people who had never before been exposed to such disease.
